title: Homily III — A third hymn for the Mother of God

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily III on the Dormition, col. 753 (PDF leaf 418)

pass_a_gloss: It is custom (ἔθος) for those erotically/passionately disposed toward something always to carry this on the tongue, and in the mind (νοῦς) by night and by day to picture [it]. Let no one then call me to account (εὐθυνέτω), if [as] third upon the preceding (προλαβοῦσι) two I made the present hymn (ἐφύμνιον) to the Mother of my God, as some departure-gift; for not gratifying her, but myself and you present, O divine and holy assembly (σύστημα), setting before [you] a dish (ὄψον) soul-profiting (ψυχωφελές) and saving (σωτήριον), suited (κατάλληλον) to this holy night, and trading for spiritual delight (θυμηδία). For scarcity of edibles (ἐδώδιμα), as you see, had seized us. Therefore indeed I improvise (σχεδιάζω) the full feast (πανδαισία), even if not lavishly (πολυτελῶς), nor worthily of her who has invited (κεκληκυῖα), but able at least necessarily (ἀναγκαίως) to console hunger (πεῖνα). For she is not in want (προσδεής) of the praises (ἐγκώμια) from us, but we in need (ἐπιδεεῖς) of the glory (δόξα) from her. For the glorified, how will it be glorified? The spring of light, how will it be illumined? But for ourselves, through what we do (δρῶμεν), we weave (πλέκομεν) a crown (στέφανος). 'For I live, says the Lord, and those glorifying me I will glorify.' Sweet indeed truly, sweet drink [is] wine, and nourishing (τρόφιμος) bread for food. For the one gladdens (εὐφραίνει), the other strengthens (στηρίζει) the heart of man. But what [is] sweeter than the Mother of my God? She took my mind captive; the tongue she plundered (ἐληΐσατο); her waking and dreaming I picture. She, Mother of the Word (Λόγος), has also become supplier (χορηγός) of word/speech (λόγος); the offspring (κύημα) of the barren woman (στεῖρα), which makes fruit-bearing the barren souls. Her holy and divine translation/passing (μετάστασις) we celebrate today. Come then, let us go up (ἀναβῶμεν) to the mystical mountain, and having become higher (ὑπέρτεροι) than the life-related (βιωτικαί) and material (ὑλικαί) appearances/impressions (ἐμφάσεις), and having entered under the divine and incomprehensible (ἄληπτος) darkness (γνόφος), having come to be in the divine light, let us hymn the infinitely-powerful power. How he who from the surpassing lofty height (περιωπή), the immaterial (ἄϋλος) and beyond (ἐπέκεινα) all, having come down into the virginal belly (νηδύς) without going out from the paternal womb (γαστήρ), both conceived (συλληφθείς) and enfleshed (σαρκωθείς), and having journeyed (ὁδεύσας) willingly (ἑκουσίως) through sufferings (πάθη) to death, and with a body having birth from earth, and having acquired (κτησάμενος) for corruption (φθορᾷ) the incorrupt (τὸ ἄφθαρτον), having gone back up (ἀναφοιτήσας) again to the Father, drew up (ἐπεσπάσατο) his Mother according to the flesh (κατὰ σάρκα) to his own Begetter (γεννήτωρ), having lifted aloft (μετεωρίσας) her who had been named an earthly heaven to the heavenly earth?
pass_b_english: It is the habit of those who love something passionately always to have it on their tongue, and to picture it in their mind by night and by day. So let no one find fault with me if, after the two that came before, I have made this present hymn a third for the Mother of my God, as a kind of parting gift. For I do this not as a favour to her, but to myself and to you who are here, O divine and holy assembly: I set before you a dish that profits the soul and brings salvation, suited to this holy night, and so I win spiritual delight. For a shortage of food, as you see, had overtaken us. That is why I am putting together this feast in haste: not lavishly, nor worthy of her who has invited us, but one that can at least comfort our hunger as need requires.

For she has no need of praises from us; it is we who need the glory that comes from her. For how can what is already glorified be glorified? How can the spring of light be given light? Rather, by what we do we weave a crown for ourselves. 'For as I live, says the Lord, those who glorify me I will glorify' (1 Samuel 2:30). Sweet indeed, sweet to drink is wine, and bread is nourishing as food; for the one gladdens, and the other strengthens the heart of man (Psalm 104:15). But what is sweeter than the Mother of my God? She has taken my mind captive; she has carried off my tongue as spoil; waking and dreaming I picture her. She is the Mother of the Word, and has become the giver of words: the child conceived by the barren woman, who makes barren souls fruitful. Hers is the holy and divine passing that we celebrate today.

Come, then, let us go up to the mystical mountain (Isaiah 2:3). Let us rise above the impressions of this life and of matter, and pass into the divine and incomprehensible darkness (Exodus 20:21), and, coming to be in the divine light, let us hymn the power that is boundless in might. How is it that he who came down from the surpassing height that is immaterial and beyond all things, into the virgin's womb, without leaving the Father's womb; who was conceived and took flesh, and of his own will travelled through sufferings to death; who won incorruption for what was corruptible, and went back up to the Father with a body that had its birth from the earth: how is it that he drew his Mother according to the flesh to his own Begetter, lifting her, who had been called an earthly heaven, up to the heavenly land?

choices.note: Printed margin: '1 Reg.

II, 30' = 1 Kingdoms LXX = 1 Samuel 2:30 (τοὺς δοξάζοντάς με δοξάσω); the opening 'For as I live, says the Lord' (Ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει Κύριος) is the common prophetic oath formula, not part of 1 Samuel 2:30, and the author joins it to the quotation; the citation stands beside the whole quoted sentence.
'Psal.
CIII, 15' is LXX/Vulgate numbering = Psalm 104:15 in English Bibles (wine gladdens, bread strengthens the heart).
Unprinted allusions cited because the wording is clear: Isaiah 2:3 (LXX Δεῦτε καὶ ἀναβῶμεν εἰς τὸ ὄρος, same words and order; also Micah 4:2);
Exodus 20:21 (Moses entering the darkness, γνόφος, where God was), the Dionysian figure of the ascent into the divine darkness.
Left uncited: 'taken my mind captive' may echo 2 Corinthians 10:5;

'the Father's womb' (πατρικὴ γαστήρ) recalls Psalm 110:3 (LXX 109:3, 'from the womb before the morning star'), a patristic way of speaking of the eternal begetting; kept literally to keep the pairing with 'the virgin's womb'.
'Τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγος τρίτος ...' heading not translated (kept out of the source row); the row title names the homily.
Variants (Migne fn64-66): σπάνη (Seg.
σπάνις), βρῶσιν (Seg.
βρωτόν), περιουσίου (Seg.
ὑπερουσίου) make no difference to the English except the last: 'surpassing height' follows the printed περιουσίου;
Seguier's ὑπερουσίου would read 'the height beyond being'.
'ἐφύμνιον' rendered 'hymn';
'δῶρον ἐξόδιον' 'parting gift' (a gift for her departure, as in the funeral sense of ἐξόδιον).
'ὄψον' (a cooked dish, relish) rendered 'a dish';
'ἐμπορευόμενος' (gain by trade) rendered 'and so I win'.
'Σπάνη ...
τῶν ἐδωδίμων' is rendered literally ('a shortage of food'); it may be a figure for the need of spiritual food, or refer to the fast before the feast, but the Greek does not say which.
'τῆς κεκληκυίας' (feminine) rendered 'her who has invited us': the Mother of God as host of the feast.
'λόγου καθέστηκε χορηγός' rendered 'has become the giver of words', keeping the Word / words play.
'τὸ τῆς στείρας κύημα' = Mary as the child of the barren Anna (see Homily I, section 1.6).
'μετάστασις' rendered 'passing'.

'φθορᾷ κτησάμενος τὸ ἄφθαρτον' rendered 'won incorruption for what was corruptible' (dative of advantage); it could also mean 'by corruption gained incorruption' (through death); the first is preferred because μετὰ σώματος ...
ἀναφοιτήσας stresses the risen body;
Migne's Latin takes the second ('incorruptione per corruptionem acquisita').
The closing 'Πῶς ...;' is the content of the hymn just announced; kept as a question, split at the participles for readability, every clause kept.
'γεννήτωρ' capitalised as 'Begetter' since it names God the Father.
'οὐρανὸν ἐπίγειον ...
ἐπουράνιον γῆν' kept as the chiasmus 'earthly heaven ... heavenly land'.
